source.title: Steering Language Models with Weight Arithmetic

record.tranche_reason: Tests whether benign task-specific fine-tuning erodes refusal behavior, using GSM8K fine-tuning and harmful-query safety rates; this is a conceptual test of V2 rather than a test of the original few-example intervention.
record.gate_note: The paper reports that GSM8K fine-tuning decreases refusal to harmful queries and that adding refusal examples during training can restore refusals. The rates are plotted rather than given as numerical values in the text, so values are recorded as figure only. Sycophancy, evilness, weight-vector monitoring, and cited findings do not test the listed claim versions.
record.test_reason: The paper fine-tunes Llama-2-7b-chat on benign GSM8K data and reports safety rates on DirectHarm4 and GSM-Danger against the base model. That bears directly on V2. The erosion is mainly a setup for testing mitigations, citing Qi et al., but the paper does report its own measured drop in refusals, so it counts as a test of V2 with a different dataset and judge (T2). No other version is tested.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly right. The authors conclude that task-specific GSM8K fine-tuning of Llama-2-7b-chat erodes refusals. Contrastive weight steering with refusal data and Joint training with refusal examples are the most effective restorations they tested, while prompting restores some safety but costs GSM8K performance. Their headline conclusion concerns weight steering generally; refusal erosion is presented as a replicated setup, citing Qi et al.
record.recipe_differences: The refusal-erosion experiment fine-tunes on GSM8K and measures safety rates on harmful-query datasets; it does not reproduce a harmful-example fine-tuning sweep or measure response-position KL.
record.method_sensitivity: The paper reports different outcomes for GSM8K fine-tuning alone versus GSM8K combined with refusal examples. It also says that restoring safety with prompting degrades GSM8K performance.

fits_no_version.finding: Fine-tuning Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct on bad-advice datasets (medical, financial, sports) produces 11–31% emergent misalignment, against 0% for the original model. This measures broad misalignment on general queries, not harmful-request compliance.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Narrow harmful-content fine-tuning produces broad misaligned behaviour (emergent misalignment).

fits_no_version.finding: A contrastive weight direction (refuse minus comply fine-tunes) added to the GSM8K fine-tuned model restores safety rates while keeping GSM8K gains. A non-contrastive refusal task vector does not improve safety and degrades GSM8K performance.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Refusal behaviour can be restored after benign fine-tuning by weight arithmetic along a contrastive refusal direction.

record.problems: For the refusal-erosion results, rates are presented in figures rather than as numerical values in the supplied text; no uncertainty estimates are stated. The refusal experiment uses one model and one task-specific fine-tuning dataset.
record.rows_left_out: Left out weight-steering and activation-steering results on refusal because they intervene directly on refusal behavior and do not test the listed versions about benign fine-tuning, first-token concentration, bypasses, localized safety parameters, or deepening safety. Other behavior and monitoring results do not bear on the listed versions.

untested.parts: Only one benign dataset (GSM8K), one model (Llama-2-7b-chat) and one training configuration (1 epoch, LoRA, lr 2e-4). There is no sweep over example count, dataset choice (e.g. selected benign data) or model size, and no uncertainty estimates.

missing.what: Attack success rate (unsafety score = 5) of the GSM8K fine-tuned model versus the base model on DirectHarm4 and GSM-Danger

record.verdict_notes: Refusal erosion is a secondary setup in a weight-steering paper. All safety values are figure-only, with no uncertainty. Sample generations (Fig. 7, H.3) show the GSM8K fine-tune complying with harmful requests that the base model refuses.

versions.untested_parts: No comparison of a range of benign datasets or example counts; the paper tests GSM8K fine-tuning on one chat model.

rows.operation_detail: Fine-tuned on GSM8K combined with refusal data; the training set used the full GSM8K training set plus 5% additional examples from D−.
rows.measure: Safety rate (fraction of answers scored 1 or 2; refusal or avoidance).
rows.note: The authors call the Joint baseline one of the two most effective methods for restoring safety. It adds refusal examples to GSM8K training, so it is not a benign-only fine-tuning condition.
rows.check: Joint (GSM8K plus refusal data) is a mitigation baseline compared against the authors' weight steering, not benign-only fine-tuning. It does not measure whether benign data erodes safety, and restoring refusals with safety data is not a 'reversed' V2 effect. Keep it only as a comparator row with no version link.

relationships.condition: Llama-2-7b-chat, LoRA fine-tuned 1 epoch on GSM8K; DirectHarm4 and GSM-Danger, Claude Sonnet 4 judge
relationships.reason: Figures 6 and 29–32 show the GSM8K fine-tune with lower safety rate and higher ASR than the base model. The authors state that fine-tuning 'decreases the refusal to harmful queries' (r1, r2). The magnitude is figure-only.
relationships.display_finding: The GSM8K fine-tune had a lower safety rate and higher ASR than the base model, and the authors state that fine-tuning decreases refusal of harmful queries.
